summary: Describes how IPv6 is supported in 3GPP's Evolved Packet System, the cellular architecture behind HSPA and LTE. Operators face a shortage of IPv4 addresses and increasing pressure to move to IPv6. It is informational guidance for the mobile world.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how a mobile device connects through a 3GPP network gateway and receives an IP address. It describes ways to use IPv4 and IPv6 together, and the technical limits that affect migration to IPv6.

subtitle: How mobile packet networks assign IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity to a device.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks need to provide IP connectivity while supporting both older IPv4-only devices and newer IPv6-capable devices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how GPRS contexts and EPS connections attach a device to a gateway, assign addresses, and carry traffic. It describes IPv4v6 connections, IPv6 address setup, and deployment constraints.
tldr.outcome: This is an informational overview of 3GPP IPv6 support as understood in January 2012. Dual-stack access preserves IPv4 connectivity but still assigns an IPv4 address to each bearer.

today: RFC 6459 is an Informational document published in January 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so its deployment discussion describes the 3GPP specifications available at that time.

sections.title: IPv6 in 3GPP Networks
sections.content:
RFC 6459 describes how Internet Protocol (IP) connectivity works in 3GPP mobile networks, including GPRS and the Evolved Packet System (EPS). It focuses on IPv6 support and the transition from IPv4, in response to IPv4 address shortages described in the document.

The RFC explains that support in specifications does not by itself ensure deployment. It aims to keep IPv4-only devices connected while allowing dual-stack devices to use IPv4 or IPv6 when their application, network connection, and destination support it.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how mobile networks connect devices to the Internet using IPv4 and IPv6. It also describes why having IPv6 in the specifications does not make the change automatic.

sections.title: Connections, Gateways, and Bearers
sections.content:
A mobile device reaches an external packet network through a gateway selected using an Access Point Name (APN). A device may connect to more than one gateway, for example to reach the Internet and an operator network. In GPRS, the connection is called a Packet Data Protocol (PDP) context; in EPS, it is a Packet Data Network (PDN) connection.

A PDP context or PDN connection acts like a network interface on the device and receives an IPv4 address, an IPv6 prefix, or both. An EPS bearer groups IP flows that receive the same packet-forwarding treatment. The default bearer carries traffic without a dedicated bearer, while dedicated bearers serve flows needing different treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: The device connects through a named gateway, and each connection acts like a network interface. In EPS, bearers group traffic that should receive the same forwarding treatment.

sections.title: Address Assignment
sections.content:
IPv4 address information is supplied during context or bearer setup. DHCPv4 is supported but optional, so a device must also support address setup through bearer signaling. For IPv6, 3GPP uses Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC); the specifications discussed here do not support stateful DHCPv6 address assignment.

The network assigns each default bearer one unique /64 IPv6 prefix. The device uses an identifier suggested through layer-2 signaling for its link-local address. The RFC also describes limits: only one /64 prefix is supported per bearer, and the prefix lifetime follows the layer-2 connection. Prefix delegation is part of Release-10; before that, the device may share its prefix using a Neighbor Discovery proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile network gives each default bearer one IPv6 /64 prefix, and the device builds addresses from it. The RFC describes limits on extra prefixes and explains that prefix delegation arrived in Release-10.

sections.title: Using IPv4 and IPv6 Together
sections.content:
Before Release-8, a device generally needed separate IPv4 and IPv6 PDP contexts for dual-stack access. Release-8 introduced an IPv4v6 PDN connection and bearer that can carry both address families; GPRS added IPv4v6 PDP contexts in Release-9. During EPS setup, the device attaches, the network authenticates it, the gateway creates the connection and assigns address information, and radio-bearer setup completes.

The RFC notes that dual-stack does not remove the need for IPv4 addresses: every dual-stack bearer still receives one. IPv6-only access is possible, but applications that require IPv4 need translation to reach IPv4 networks. Handover between networks with different capabilities can also require the operator to use only a common address type.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer mobile networks can carry IPv4 and IPv6 on one bearer; older networks may need separate connections. Dual-stack helps preserve access for older systems, but it still consumes IPv4 addresses.

sections.title: Link Behavior and Deployment Limits
sections.content:
The radio-side connection resembles a point-to-point link without link-layer addresses. The RFC describes operating-system and gateway behaviors that can interrupt IPv6, such as discarding Router Advertisements or failing to complete Neighbor Discovery. If address resolution does not finish, IPv6 traffic can stall.

Private IPv4 address pools may be reused across gateways or network areas when one unique address per subscriber is not available. IPv6-only service also depends on application support, network configuration, and roaming arrangements. The RFC concludes that applications and solutions should be tested before relying on IPv6-only access.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile links do not behave exactly like ordinary Ethernet links, so some device software may mishandle IPv6 setup. IPv6-only service also needs compatible applications and network support, especially when a device roams.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the document introduces no new security concerns. During network attachment, the device and network authenticate each other. The control plane has at least integrity and replay protection, while protection of user traffic and parts of the network depends on the operator's deployment.

The point-to-point link model limits some on-link attacks because the device and first-hop router are the only nodes on that link. The RFC says off-link IPv6 attacks remain comparable to those in other IPv6 systems. It prohibits using a permanent subscriber identity such as an IMSI in an IPv6 interface identifier because that could enable tracking.
sections.plainLanguage: The device and mobile network authenticate during attachment, and control messages receive integrity protection. A device must not use its permanent subscriber identity to form an IPv6 address.
